full_judgment:
4. As Mr. Abdur Rab-1 raised a preliminary objection as to maintainability of the petition he is heard first. In support of affidavit-in-opposition he referred me to the various papers viz., the annexures, the judgments, the statements of budget and the relevant provision of the Ordinance to contend that in spite of incorporation of the petitioner as a limited company under the Companies Act the petitioner retains its position and character as a Public Sector Enterprises and section 162 of the Companies Act, 1913 has got no role to play in respect of public Sector Enterprises and as such this petition is liable to be dismissed in limini. A close reading of section 162(1) of the Act seems that a company may be wound up by court if the company has resolved by a special resolution for its winding up. In order to invoke the provision of section 162(i) of the Companies Act, 1913 the first condition to be satisfied by the petitioner that the company to be wound up is a company within the meaning of companies Act. According to section 3 of the Companies Act, 1913 a 'Company' means a company formed and registered under the Companies Act, 1913 or an existing company. On reference to this petition as well as affidavit-in-opposition it appears that there is no denial that the company in submitting statement under sections 32 and 104 of the Companies Act, 1913 violated the provisions of law and was served with a notice to show cause for .imposing penalty upon the Managing Director of the company by the Registrar of the Joint Stock Company. This vital fact cannot be ignored in deciding the question of maintainability. It is also pertinent to note that no objection was laid before the Registrar of Joint Stock Company against the application for incorporation of the petitioner company as such. Mr. Rab, however placing reliance on section 2(d) and the Schedule of the Ordinance No. 48 of 1986 submits that the company is not a public company and it is public company and is public Corporation and public Sector Enterprise. The Public Corporation (Management Co-ordination) Ordinance,1986 (Ordinance 48 of 1986) in the preamble to provide for the co-ordination of management of the affairs and business of certain public corporation the President is pleased to make and promulgate the Ordinance. "Section 2(d) of the Ordinance says "Public Corporation" means an authority, body, organisation or company specified in the schedule to this Ordinance. Thus, it is seen that although the Ordinance was promulgated for corporation and certain Public Corporation the definition included a company. Now whether the contention of Mr. Rab that for the placement of the company under Sl. No. 32 of the said Schedule the petitioner is not a company can be accepted, I am afraid to accept the contention of Mr. Rab that for such placement the petitioner company becomes a Public Sector Corporation. According to me, section 162 of the Companies Act read with section 2(d) and the Schedule of Ordinance No. 48 of 1986 the petitioner in all respects satisfies the qualifications of a Company and this petition for winding up pursuant to the Special Resolution passed in the Council Meeting of the Ministers is competent. To support my conclusion one thing must be noted and it is Sl. No. 32 which also makes reference to "company Limited" and not "Public Sector Enterprises". Mr. Rab placing reliance on serial No. 37 of the list of the members of the Consultative Committee of Public Enterprises contends that as per Sl. No. 37 Mr. AFM Abdus Salam is the Managing Director of the Bangladesh Consumer Supplies Co. Ltd. and that the journal relates to Public Enterprise and in the Gazette the company is not included as the solitary Enterprise but it contains as many as 16 companies, Enterprises etc. and as such the petitioner is not a company and it is either a Public Enterprises on corporation. My reading of this document is contrary to what Mr. Rab contends in view of the fact of incorporation of the company under Companies Act, 1913 and the definitions of the Company as given in section 2 of the Companies Act and 2(d) of Public Corporation (Management and co-ordination) Ordinance, 1986. In this view of the law and facts of this case I hold the petitioner is a company in spite of the fact that in the list of the members of the consultative committee of public Enterprises the name of the company is included. 

 5. Mr. Md. Abu Yusuf, in his affidavit-in-opposition, has stated that as the Government assured to retain him he did not take further step except filing the leave petition from the judgment of Writ Petition. He also describes him as a creditor. I do not understand having described him so how he raises objection on maintainability of the petition in that the description as creditor itself connotes that he is a creditor of a company which is unable to pay its debt. In the case if the company goes into liquidation his claim will remain. It is consistently held by the superior courts of this subcontinent that a creditor cannot compel a company to run its business at loss and cannot thwart the petition for winding up of a company. Thus, the petitioning company in this case which has been running at a loss to the tune of about Taka 21 crore from 1980-89 specially when this statement of loss has not been controverted by affidavit-in-opposition, cannot be forced to run its business only at further loss. It is pertinent to point out that the Government can do business apart from functioning as a department or organ of the State. In this case I do not find anything to say that the business run by the company is not a trading or a commercial business and the petitioner is working in the administrative capacity of the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Here in doing the business the company is not at all concerned with performance of the Governmental function and its activities being commercial and trading in nature it cannot be regarded as a department or organ of the State. Where the Government is engaged in doing commercial or trading business through a company owned by it, like the present one, I hold that the company satisfies all the qualifications of a company within the meaning of Companies Act, 1913 and the petition for its winding up is competent, if otherwise not in competent or fails. The observation of the Appellate Division made in the case of New Dhaka Ltd. Vs. Qumrul Huda and others, 31 DLR (AD) 234 cited by Mr. Alimuzzaman Chowdhury supports me. 

 7. The application filed by one Md. Mosharaf Hossain for accepting the salami money regarding shop Nos. 10 and 11 of Bhawal Bipani Bitan, Gazipur by the Gazipur Zilla Parishad is totally misconceived in view of the facts and circumstance of the present case and is hereby rejected.
